title: United States ex rel. D’Agostino Excavators, Inc. v. Heyward-Robinson Co. (1970)
summary: The interrelated administration of two construction jobs supported treating the second-job claims as compulsory counterclaims.
notes:
This predates § 1367. A present course analysis should examine the statute discussed elsewhere in the assigned chapter rather than assume every aspect of older ancillary-jurisdiction terminology supplies the statutory answer.

D'Agostino sued Heyward and its surety, Maryland Casualty Company, under the Miller Act for payments due on the Navy barracks job at the New London submarine base; Heyward counterclaimed for overpayments and extra completion costs on both the Navy job and the private Stelma plant job in Stamford, and the Second Circuit affirmed the judgment.

sections.Parties: D’Agostino, a subcontractor, sued prime contractor Heyward-Robinson and its surety concerning a federal construction project; the parties also disputed a private project.
sections.Material Facts: The subcontractor performed excavation work on a Navy project and on a separate private job. The dealings were linked by insurance arrangements, payments that were not consistently allocated to only one project, and communications or termination decisions affecting both. Although the physical projects were distinct, the business dispute could not readily be separated into two unrelated accounts.
sections.Procedural History: The litigation produced a jury award involving the parties’ accounts. On appeal, the court considered whether the private-project counterclaims properly belonged in the federal case and upheld their treatment as compulsory.
sections.Issue: Did the private-project claims arise from the same transaction or occurrence as the claim concerning the federal project?
sections.Holding: The majority held that they did, applying a logical-relationship approach to the connected dealings.
sections.Reasoning: The majority evaluated the commercial relationship and factual overlap rather than requiring the claims to concern the same physical construction site or contract instrument. The linked administration of the jobs made joint adjudication sensible and supported ancillary jurisdiction under the doctrine then in use. The decision therefore shows both the breadth of a transaction test and the need to distinguish procedural classification from the source of federal judicial power.

learning.why: The interrelated administration of two construction jobs supported treating the second-job claims as compulsory counterclaims.

topics.cp-counterclaim: The majority treated the private-project dispute as compulsory because of its logical relationship to the federal-project dispute.
topics.cp-transaction: Shared payment, insurance, and termination arrangements connected otherwise distinct construction projects.
topics.cp-supplemental: The opinion’s ancillary-jurisdiction reasoning must be read in its pre-§ 1367 setting.
topics.cp-frcp-13: The case construes 'transaction or occurrence' in Rule 13(a) and the compulsory/permissive line.
topics.cp-supplemental-history: The court upheld jurisdiction over the Stelma counterclaims as ancillary to the Miller Act claim, the pre-§ 1367 doctrine for counterclaims.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Friendly agreed with the result but questioned classifying the second project’s claims as compulsory. His separate reasoning favored jurisdiction over the related dispute without stretching the compulsory-counterclaim label.

mnemonic.rationale: Navy barracks and a Miller Act claim
